title: Arrays
summary: An array is an ordered list of values.

subtopics.title: Create a list
subtopics.explanation: An array stores an ordered list of values in square brackets, such as `["tea", "bread"]`. It is useful when items belong together and their position matters. A shopping list is a familiar example. Arrays can contain objects too, such as a list of product records returned by an API. Arrays preserve item order and can grow or shrink. Use an array when position or iteration matters, and use an object when values are better identified by names. Think of an array as a numbered shopping list: order matters, and each item has a position.

subtopics.title: Indexes
subtopics.explanation: Indexes start at zero, so `items[0]` reads the first item. The last index is `items.length - 1`; an empty array has no last item. Check the length before reading a calculated position. This prevents `undefined` values from appearing when a list has no matching records. An index can be outside the current bounds after a list changes. Check the array’s length before reading a computed position. An array index is like a seat number that starts at zero.

subtopics.title: List size
subtopics.explanation: `.length` gives the number of items, not the last index. For a three-item array, length is 3 and the final index is 2. Use it to check whether a collection is empty or control a loop. Do not assume a list always contains at least one item. Length updates when items are added or removed. A loop should compare its index against the current length and avoid modifying the collection unexpectedly. Think of a theater: length counts the seats, while the final seat number is one less.

subtopics.title: Transform with map
subtopics.explanation: `.map()` calls a function for each item and returns a new array of transformed results. For example, map product records to the labels shown in a dropdown. Use it when each input should produce one output. Avoid map for side effects when a loop communicates the intent more clearly. Map creates a new outer array, but object items inside are still references. Avoid mutating those objects if other code shares them. Map is like passing every item through the same label maker.

subtopics.title: Choose with filter
subtopics.explanation: `.filter()` returns a new array containing only items that pass a test. For example, filter tasks to keep those not yet completed. The original array remains unchanged, though nested objects are still shared references. Design an empty state for the case where no items pass the filter. Filter preserves the relative order of matching items. A predicate should be clear and side-effect free so the resulting list is predictable. Filter is like keeping only the papers that pass a checklist.

foundations.overview: An array stores an ordered list of values. JavaScript arrays are useful when items belong together and their position matters, such as search results or a shopping list. Think of an array like numbered slots in a row. Use methods such as `map` to create transformed lists and `filter` to keep matching items, and avoid mutating shared data accidentally.
foundations.whyItMatters: Arrays appear in API results, form choices, and component lists. Their ordering and mutation behavior affect rendering, so use the right method for each transformation.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine often stores arrays with contiguous, packed elements for fast indexed access; introducing holes or mixing types can force a slower, dictionary-style representation. So consistent, packed arrays read fastest.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Rendering lists of UI components, holding API result sets, queues and stacks, accumulating values in a reduce, and representing grids or matrices all use arrays.
foundations.businessImpact: Efficient list handling powers responsive feeds, tables, and search results; mishandling large arrays (or accidental mutations) shows up as sluggish UIs and data bugs.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing which methods mutate vs copy, and how indexing and length behave, prevents subtle data-corruption bugs and makes data transformations clean and predictable.
foundations.performanceImpact: End operations (push/pop) are fast; front operations (shift/unshift) re-index everything and are slower. Packed arrays beat sparse ones, and unnecessary copies cost memory in hot loops.
commonUseCases: Storing and rendering lists of items (search results, table rows, menus)
Implementing stacks and queues with push/pop/shift
Accumulating or transforming data with map, filter, and reduce
Modeling grids and matrices with nested arrays

commonMisconceptions.myth: splice and slice do roughly the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: slice returns a copy and leaves the original untouched; splice mutates the original in place and returns the removed items.

commonMisconceptions.myth: typeof [] tells you something is an array.
commonMisconceptions.reality: typeof [] is 'object' because arrays are objects — use Array.isArray() to actually test for an array.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Calling map changes the original array.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Map returns a new array; changes inside its callback can still mutate referenced objects.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An index starts at one because it is the first position.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript arrays are zero-indexed, so the first position is zero and the last is length minus one.

visualExplorer.title: How an array changes as you mutate it
visualExplorer.caption: Step through creating an array and watch indices and length update as you push, pop, and splice.

config.intro: Follow an array of fruits through indexing and the core mutating methods.

steps.name: Create with a literal
steps.detail: const fruits = ['apple', 'banana'] makes a length-2 array: index 0 is 'apple', index 1 is 'banana'.

steps.name: Read by index
steps.detail: fruits[0] returns 'apple'; an out-of-range index like fruits[5] returns undefined, not an error.

steps.name: push to the end
steps.detail: fruits.push('cherry') appends at index 2; length becomes 3. push is fast because nothing re-indexes.

steps.name: unshift to the front
steps.detail: fruits.unshift('mango') inserts at index 0, shifting every other element up one index; length becomes 4.

steps.name: splice to edit in place
steps.detail: fruits.splice(1, 1) removes 1 element at index 1, mutating the array and returning the removed item.

steps.name: Check length
steps.detail: length always reflects the current count — one more than the highest index — after every change.

interactiveExamples.title: Indexing and the core methods
interactiveExamples.explanation: Create an array, read by index, then add and remove at both ends while watching length.

sandbox.code:
const fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];

console.log(fruits[0]); // apple
console.log(fruits.at(-1)); // cherry
console.log(fruits.length); // 3

fruits.push('date'); // add to end
fruits.shift(); // remove from front
console.log(fruits); // ['banana', 'cherry', 'date']

interactiveExamples.title: slice vs splice
interactiveExamples.explanation: slice returns a copy and leaves the original alone; splice mutates the original in place.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: [2,3], unchanged original, then removed [2,3] and mutated [1,'x',4,5].

codeLab.title: Remove duplicates from an array
codeLab.instructions: Implement unique(arr) that returns a new array with duplicates removed, preserving first-seen order. Do not mutate the input. A Set or a tracking array both work.
hints: A Set automatically discards duplicate values while keeping insertion order.
Spread the Set back into an array with [...new Set(arr)].

keyTakeaways: An array stores an ordered list of values in square brackets, such as `["tea", "bread"]`.
Indexes start at zero, so `items[0]` reads the first item.
